title: AI Can Now Spend Your Money. Are We Ready for What Comes Next?
summary: Discover how ChatGPT Wallet is changing agentic commerce and raising new questions about AI payments, security, and consumer trust.
body_markdown:
The launch of ChatGPT Wallet marks an important shift in commerce. AI is moving from recommending what we should buy to participating in the transaction itself. OpenAI says users approve purchases while payment networks provide tokenized credentials, meaning the AI agent never receives the user’s actual card details.


[\[openai.com\]](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-wallet/)


That sounds secure. It also raises a much bigger question:


**At what point does convenience become surrendering too much control?**


Today, a person still approves each transaction. But imagine telling an AI agent, “You can spend up to $2,000 a month on approved business expenses.” Now we’re no longer talking about a smarter checkout experience. We’re talking about giving software financial authority.


And that’s when things get interesting.


## Who Is Responsible When AI Makes the Wrong Purchase?


Imagine an agent is authorized to purchase airline tickets under $1,000. It finds a $700 flight and books it. Technically, the AI followed the instructions. But the ticket is nonrefundable, the arrival time is terrible, the traveler misses an important meeting, and there was a much better flight available for $750.


Was the transaction successful?


The payment processor would probably say yes. The user might say absolutely not.


**When AI starts making purchasing decisions, “authorized” and “correct” may become two very different things.**


So who owns the mistake? The consumer who established the rules? The AI provider? The merchant? The issuing bank? The payment network? The company that authorized the agent to spend?


We’ve spent decades developing protections around unauthorized transactions. Agentic commerce could introduce something much murkier:


**a perfectly authorized transaction that the customer never would have made.**


## What Does Fraud Look Like When the Buyer Is an AI Agent?


Fraud systems traditionally evaluate people, accounts, devices and transactions. Agentic commerce adds another participant to the equation: the AI itself.


Was the agent authorized? What was it permitted to purchase? Did it stay within its spending limits? Were its instructions altered? Could a malicious website manipulate an agent into purchasing something the user never intended?


That leads to an uncomfortable question:


**Could the AI agent itself become the new attack surface?**


If criminals don’t need to steal your credit card because they can manipulate the software authorized to use it,


[fraud prevention](https://usio.com/faster-money-smarter-fraud-ai-buyers-synthetic-identities-and-the-new-rules-of-trust/) becomes an entirely different challenge.


## Who Controls What the Agent Chooses?


This could become one of the biggest debates surrounding agentic commerce.


Ask an AI agent to “find me the best hotel in Chicago for under $300.” Which hotel does it choose?


Does it choose the objectively best option? The hotel with the best structured data? The merchant whose website is easiest for an agent to navigate? A preferred commercial partner? A sponsored result? A company offering the


[AI platform](https://usio.com/which-payment-processors-support-an-ai-platform/) better economics?


We’ve spent years debating paid search rankings, marketplace placement, sponsored content and retail media. But what happens when consumers don’t see all the choices in the first place?


**If an AI evaluates 500 products and presents one, how much influence does the algorithm suddenly have over the point of purchase?**


That could make visibility to AI agents as important as visibility in traditional search.


## Could Merchants Become Invisible?


OpenAI says businesses will maintain their customer relationships and retain control over pricing, fulfillment, returns and customer service.


[\[openai.com\]](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-wallet/)


But what happens as agents become increasingly autonomous?


Imagine telling your AI agent, “Keep my pantry stocked.” From that point forward, the agent chooses when to order, what to purchase, which merchant gets the order and potentially which payment method to use.


If that happens,


**does the consumer really have a relationship with the merchant anymore, or does the AI platform increasingly control that relationship?**


Every retailer, marketplace and software company should be thinking about that question now.


## What Happens to Brand Loyalty?


This may be one of the most fascinating questions for marketers.


Companies spend billions creating preference through advertising, packaging, storytelling, content, loyalty programs, search visibility and customer experience. That strategy assumes a human ultimately makes the decision.


But an AI agent may evaluate an entirely different set of criteria: price, availability, delivery speed, return policies, ratings, contractual terms or whatever factors its user tells it to prioritize.


So what happens when


**your customer isn’t choosing your brand anymore? Their agent is.**


Do companies eventually market to algorithms as aggressively as they market to people?


Search engines gave us search engine optimization. Answer engines introduced answer engine optimization. Agentic commerce could create the next discipline:


**optimizing your business to become the transaction AI chooses.**


## Could AI Change Payment Economics?


There’s another question worth debating: What happens when AI can evaluate payment economics before every transaction?


Imagine an agent comparing four merchants in seconds. Merchant A charges $102 with free shipping. Merchant B charges $98 plus shipping. Merchant C charges $101 but offers better rewards. Merchant D provides a discount when the buyer selects a different payment method.


A human may never calculate all those variables. An AI agent can.


Now apply that same capability to business purchasing, where companies manage thousands of invoices, multiple vendors, different payment methods, transaction fees, payment terms, incentives and settlement speeds.


AI could eventually optimize not just


**what to buy** , but


**how to pay for it** .


What happens to processing economics when software can evaluate the cost of every payment option before initiating a transaction? Could AI agents begin steering transactions toward lower-cost payment methods? Could merchants offer incentives specifically designed to influence an agent’s decision?


The battle for the transaction could look very different when software is doing the math.


## What Happens When AI Agents Start Transacting With Other AI Agents?


Perhaps the biggest question is what happens when both sides of the transaction become automated.


Today, we’re talking about a human asking an AI agent to make a purchase from a business. But eventually, we could see a buyer’s AI agent interacting directly with a seller’s AI agent.


The buyer’s agent identifies the product. Another agent negotiates price. A business system verifies inventory. Another system approves the expense. A payment agent determines the preferred payment method and initiates the transaction.


Humans establish the rules, but they may never participate in the individual transaction.


**What happens to commerce when software begins negotiating, buying, selling and paying other software?**


More importantly, what happens to the infrastructure underneath those transactions?


## The Real Opportunity May Be Trust


The winners in agentic commerce may not simply be the companies that build the smartest AI agents. They could be the companies that provide the trust infrastructure underneath them.


Who authorized the agent? What exactly was it authorized to do? How much can it spend? Where can it spend? How long does that authority last? Can permission be revoked instantly? How do we prove the agent followed the rules? How do merchants distinguish legitimate agents from malicious bots? Who is responsible when something goes wrong?


These aren’t simply AI questions. They’re


**payments, identity, security, risk, compliance and authorization questions.**


And that could create an enormous opportunity for payment companies, networks, banks, fintechs and embedded payment providers.


## We’re Not Just Giving AI a Wallet. We’re Giving It Authority.


It’s easy to look at ChatGPT Wallet and see another digital wallet.


I think that’s too small.


AI first helped us search. Then it helped us compare. Then it helped us decide. Now it can participate in the transaction. ChatGPT Wallet gives agents a secure mechanism to pay on a user’s behalf while requiring the user to authorize the purchase.


[\[openai.com\]](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-wallet/)


The much more consequential step comes when we begin telling AI:


**“You don’t need to ask me every time. Here are the rules. Stay within them.”**


At that point, we aren’t simply giving AI a new payment method.


**We’re giving software authority over money.**


And that leaves the payments industry with a much bigger question:


**When money starts moving automatically, who do we trust to establish, enforce and verify the rules?**


Agentic commerce is coming.


The technology may actually be the easy part.


**Trust will be much harder.**
